correctness.rationale: Taking successive increments is a determinant-one map from the anchored ball to the cube slab. Independently of the frozen Fourier calculation, integration by parts in one uniform coordinate gives E[S_d φ(S_d)]=(d/2)E[(1−Z_1²)φ′(S_d)]. Compact support then gives the density for the latter second-moment defect as (2/d)∫_|s|^d x h_d(x) dx; integrating it over the slab yields exactly v, while b follows from h_d. For the strict sign, the remaining-sum acceptance g(w) is even and nonincreasing in |w|. When d≥4 its derivative is negative for some w in (0,2): the density of the other d−2 uniforms is strictly decreasing on its positive support, and one can take |t−w|<d−2 since t<d. For d=3 there is a subinterval with |t−w|<1<t+w where the uniform convolution decreases, and for d=2 g is an indicator with its jump at t<2. Thus g(x+y)<g(x−y) on a positive-measure subset of (0,1)². Pairing opposite signs in E[Z_1Z_2] gives η<0; at t=d conditioning is vacuous. The eigenvalues of increment covariance are δ and μ>0 by full-dimensional support. Cumulative summation gives the covariance kernel, and Dᵀ1=e_d gives the precision correction and the determinant from the eigenvalues. For positive limiting event probability, endpoint continuity justifies conditioned Donsker convergence and the independent Brownian bridge/truncated-normal decomposition. Fourth moments give uniform integrability for b/d and conditional concentration of the average squared increments gives v→1/3; these yield both scaled covariance and precision limits. The determinant and volume normalization then give 1/√12. At vanishing ratio the CLT gives vanishing volume only, not a path limit.
residual_risks: Precision zeros describe the inverse covariance, not non-Gaussian conditional independence. The functional limit at arbitrary vanishing-probability conditioning is not assessed or claimed.

evidence: The unit-edge cactus theorem gives L_w^+ covariance and L_w precision for centered potentials. Alexander et al. analyze finite-metric volume products, and De Bruyne et al. give bridge sampling for fixed endpoints.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The cactus theorem is broader in graph class, but unit lengths cover only t=1 on the present cycle. Volume products and bridge sampling do not give variable weighted-cycle bulk precision.

evidence: On a unit cycle the omitted edge has the same second moment as a path edge, so b=v, δ=(d+1)v/d=a_(d+1), and γ=1/δ. The cactus result then gives the same grounded cycle precision at t=1. At general t this edge symmetry is lost.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Donsker and Gaussian regression explain the path limit; the rank-one inverse is routine once exchangeable moments are known. Neither the unit-edge precision nor the all-weight volume supplies the nonredundant sign or the variable-t moment evaluation used to extract the terminal precision scaling.

value.rationale: The exact inverse covariance answers whether the shortest-path cycle's closing edge leaves a nonzero precision signature under uniform volume, including when it becomes redundant. One-dimensional formulas resolve this for all real closing lengths, and the scaled terminal coefficient describes how the signature persists at the same crossover scale as the endpoint law. This is a motivated matrix invariant beyond the known scalar volume and unit-edge case.
residual_risks: The result neither supplies graph recovery for arbitrary weighted graphs nor an arbitrary thin-slab path limit.
